record.paper_title: Grothendieck’s inequality and completely correlation preserving functions - a summary of recent results and an indication of related research problems
record.original_question: Develop a structural theory of ordinary partial Bell polynomials sufficient for Taylor-series inversion problems arising from non-completely-correlation-preserving inverse functions, including closed-form or computationally effective descriptions of the Bell-polynomial values that enter the inverse coefficients β_n; methods may include high-performance computing, algebraic software, and induction principles stronger than ordinary induction when appropriate.

evidence.quote: The strong difficulties are twofold: already in the one-dimensional case we need to know the explicit value of all of the Fourier coefficients ⟨b, Hn⟩γ1, together with a closed form expression (if available at all) of all of the coefficients βn, where the latter involves (in general, unknown values of) ordinary partial Bell polynomials. It appears to us that in general one cannot use proofs by standard induction on n ∈ N to verify statements about Bell polynomials. Here, the Noetherian Induction Principle seems to be more appropriate.

Therefore, given the intrinsic combinatoric and computational complexity regarding the determination of the Taylor series coefficients of the Taylor series of the non-CCP function gb (via the Fa´ a-di Bruno formula), related research problems (which actually do not require any knowledge of the Grothendieck inequality) could be the following ones:
(1-RP2) Continue to investigate the structure of partial Bell polynomials; possibly with the aid of high-performance computers and related (algebraic) software tools.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For integers $n\ge 1$ and $1\le k\le n$, the ordinary partial Bell polynomial in the indeterminates $x_1,x_2,\dots$ is defined by
$$
\hat B_{n,k}(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_{n-k+1}) \;=\; \sum \frac{k!}{j_1!\,j_2!\cdots j_{n-k+1}!}\, x_1^{j_1}x_2^{j_2}\cdots x_{n-k+1}^{j_{n-k+1}},
$$
where the sum runs over all tuples $(j_1,\dots,j_{n-k+1})$ of non-negative integers satisfying
$$
j_1+j_2+\cdots+j_{n-k+1}=k,\qquad j_1+2j_2+\cdots+(n-k+1)j_{n-k+1}=n.
$$
Suppose $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge 1} a_n z^n$ is a formal power series with $a_1\ne 0$, and let $g(z)=\sum_{n\ge 1}\beta_n z^n$ denote its compositional inverse. By the Faà di Bruno formula one has the closed-form representation
$$
\beta_n \;=\; \frac{1}{n\, a_1^n}\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(-1)^k\,\frac{(n+k-1)!}{(n-1)!}\,\hat B_{n-1,k}\!\left(\tfrac{a_2}{a_1},\tfrac{a_3}{a_1},\dots\right),\qquad n\ge 2.
$$

Develop a structural theory of the ordinary partial Bell polynomials $\hat B_{n,k}$ that is strong enough to yield closed-form, or otherwise computationally effective, descriptions of the values $\hat B_{n,k}(x_1,\dots,x_{n-k+1})$ entering the inversion coefficients $\beta_n$ above, in a generality sufficient to handle Taylor-series inversion of analytic functions whose coefficient sequences are not assumed to satisfy any complete-correlation-preservation property. Provide such a theory together with: (i) explicit recursive or closed-form identities for the family $\{\hat B_{n,k}\}$ that reduce the combinatorial complexity of the sum defining $\beta_n$, (ii) inductive frameworks (potentially stronger than ordinary induction on $n\in\mathbb{N}$, such as Noetherian induction on a suitable well-founded order on multi-indices) that allow the verification of structural statements about $\hat B_{n,k}$, and (iii) algorithmic procedures, possibly based on computer algebra, that compute $\hat B_{n,k}$ and the resulting $\beta_n$ efficiently for large $n$.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open research program on the structural and computational theory of ordinary partial Bell polynomials in the context of formal power-series inversion. While many identities for partial Bell polynomials are known in the combinatorics literature, no comprehensive closed-form theory addressing the specific inversion-coefficient problem described here has been identified, and the question is naturally open-ended.
